what_it_does: Static random-access memory (SRAM) chips — the fast, small scratch-pad memory inside processors — degrade over years of use as electrical stress slowly shifts the voltage thresholds of the tiny transistors inside each memory cell. Chip manufacturers test for this future degradation by deliberately applying harsher-than-normal voltages during quality checks, a technique called predictive aging testing. The problem is that current methods apply the same harsh stress uniformly to all operations (reading and writing), which is unnecessarily brutal for some operations and ends up incorrectly flagging perfectly good chips as defective. This paper identifies that SRAM cells behave asymmetrically: cells that have been storing a zero for a long time are more likely to fail when you try to read them as a one, while write operations age differently. By applying the harsh test voltage selectively — aggressively only where it models real-world aging and more gently elsewhere — the method reduces false rejections. A statistical sampling and simulation approach is also proposed to make the new testing procedure fast enough to be practical in manufacturing.
